p.src:
The corresponding derivative of a vector is not introduced as a separate rule to memorize. It follows from the metric. Begin with $V^n=g^{np}V_p.$ Then $\begin{aligned}
\nabla_m V^n
&=\nabla_m\!\left(g^{np}V_p\right) \\
&=(\nabla_m g^{np})V_p+g^{np}\nabla_m V_p \\
&=g^{np}\left(\partial_mV_p-\Gamma^r{}_{mp}V_r\right),\end{aligned}$ where metric compatibility removed the first term. Reorganizing the indices gives $\nabla_m V^n
=
\partial_m V^n+\Gamma^n{}_{mr}V^r.$

+2g_{mn}V^m\frac{DV^n}{d\lambda}\\

p.src: A geodesic has two related descriptions. Globally, it is a stationary path of the length or proper-time functional. Locally, it is the straightest possible path. The word stationary is important: depending on the geometry and endpoints, the path need not be the unique global minimum. In Lorentzian spacetime, timelike geodesics locally maximize proper time rather than minimize a positive distance.

Moreover, constant Newtonian coordinate acceleration cannot continue indefinitely: it would eventually predict a speed greater than light.

en: Is the apparent gravitational field real?

p.src: It is real as an accelerometer reading for an observer held at fixed Rindler position, but it is not invariant curvature. What cannot be eliminated over a finite region is a tidal field, represented by nonzero curvature.
